 What Does Qi2 25W Wireless Charging Mean for Your iPhone 17?

 With a compatible wireless charging setup, the iPhone 17 Qi2.2 experience looks like this: about 50% charge in roughly 25 minutes, and a quick 10-minute session can get you back to 25%. For context, standard Qi2 15W wireless charging tops out far lower.

 More power per minute. At 25W, the coil pushes roughly two-thirds more energy into the phone than a Qi2 15W charger. That is the single biggest reason top-ups finish faster.

 Smart negotiation. The charger and iPhone talk over the Qi2.2 protocol to settle on the best power level for the connected device, so the phone never pulls more than it can handle.

 What Is Qi2.2 Wireless Charging? A Detailed Breakdown
 To understand Qi2.2, it helps to see how the standard evolved. The Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) introduced the original Qi standard in 2010, establishing a universal foundation for wireless charging. Qi2 arrived in 2023, integrating magnetic alignment technology (Magnetic Power Profile, or MPP) to ensure perfect device-to-charger positioning. Now, Qi2.2—officially released by the WPC in Spring 2025—raises the power ceiling from 15W to 25W and introduces strict thermal requirements.

 How Does Qi2.2 Deliver 25W Wireless Charging?
 Hitting 25W wirelessly isn't just about cranking up the power—it requires a tightly integrated system of hardware and software working in perfect sync. Here's how Qi2.2 actually makes it happen.
 MPP 2.0: Precision That Prevents Waste
 The secret to Qi2.2's speed lies in its Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) 2.0 system. While earlier wireless pads required careful positioning to avoid energy loss, Qi2.2 uses a ring of magnets that snap your iPhone into the exact optimal position—with ±0.5 mm precision.
 This isn't just about convenience—it's about efficiency. When the coils are perfectly aligned, less energy dissipates as heat and more flows directly into your battery. At 25W, even a slight misalignment would cause significant power loss and overheating.
 EDC: The Smart Negotiator
 Extended Data Communication (EDC) is the brain behind the operation. It enables real-time dialogue between your iPhone and the charger, dynamically negotiating voltage and current based on battery level and thermal conditions.
 This isn't a one-size-fits-all handshake—it's a continuous conversation that adjusts power delivery second by second. By enabling real-time thermal monitoring and precise foreign object detection, EDC dynamically regulates power delivery to prevent overheating, ensuring safe and reliable 25W charging at all times.
 The Thermal Challenge—and Why Active Cooling Matters
 At 25W, electromagnetic coil energy loss generates significant heat. Here's the physics problem: electromagnetic coil losses generate heat roughly proportional to the square of the current. Jumping from 15W to 25W doesn't just produce 67% more heat—it can more than double it.
 Without active cooling, the charger's internal temperature would spike, forcing the system to throttle power back to 15W or lower within minutes. That's why Qi2.2 mandates a strict 40°C surface temperature limit—and why the best chargers integrate fans or thermoelectric cooling to sustain full 25W output without compromising safety or battery health.

 USB-C port wired charging

 MagSafe wireless charging

 In everyday use, it simply behaves like a cable you don't need to think about: durable, reliable, and safe for every device you charge.
 MagSafe Charger

 This Anker 3-in-1 Cube with Qi2 is a neat way to charge your iPhone , Apple Watch , and AirPods at the same time, all without cables.
 It's an official Made for MagSafe charger, so your iPhone 17 snaps into place with proper alignment and charges at 15W MagSafe speeds . The other sides of the cube pop out to reveal charging spots for your watch and earbuds.
 It pops up your iPhone 17 into an adjustable stand with up to 60° tilt , so it's easy to glance at notifications, use StandBy mode, or watch a quick video while the phone charges.
 The whole unit folds into a compact cube that fits in a small bag or even a large pocket. One outlet and one cable take care of your core Apple setup, which is perfect for hotel stays or a small bedside table.
 Qi2 25W wireless charger
 Anker Prime Wireless Charging Station (Qi2 25W, 3-in-1 Stand) 
 This Anker Prime Wireless Charging Station is built for people who want fast, reliable wireless charging and a tidy setup for their iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods. It uses the latest Qi2 25W-certified magnetic charging , which can take an iPhone 17 Pro to around 50% in about 22 minutes , so you get speeds that feel close to wired charging.
 The stand's sleek V-rod design supports your phone at a comfortable angle for StandBy mode or quick glances at notifications. And it's Apple-certified for fast charging your Apple Watch .
 On top of that, it includes several features that make everyday charging easier:
 Aerospace-grade TEC active cooling: A small thermal-electric module sits behind the charging surface to keep your phone below 89°F while charging. Lower heat helps preserve long-term battery health and keeps charging speeds consistent.
 ActiveShield 5.0 safety: The station monitors temperature more than 10 million times a day , adjusting power when needed to maintain safe, steady charging.

 It uses strong MagGo-style alignment, so your iPhone 17 stays locked in place even on bumpy roads . It also has AirCool active cooling , which helps maintain steady charging performance on hot days or during navigation.
 With 25W wireless speed, your phone can gain a meaningful amount of charge even on short drives, much faster than older 7.5W or 15W car chargers.
 Power bank

 If you travel with a laptop and your iPhone 17, this Anker Prime Power Bank (26K) can act like a mobile wall outlet.

 What Should I Pay Attention to When Charging the iPhone 17?
 Charging the iPhone 17 is simple, but a few habits can help your battery stay healthy and your charging stay fast.
 Keep an eye on heat
 iPhones charge best when they stay cool. Heat is the main thing that wears down lithium-ion batteries over time.
 Try to charge in a cool spot with some airflow.
 Avoid charging under pillows, blankets, or in direct sunlight.
 If the phone feels hot, remove the case or move it somewhere cooler.
 Heavy apps, like games or long video recordings, also add extra heat, so try not to run them while fast charging.
 Let iOS handle battery protection
 The iPhone 17 has several built-in tools that protect battery health in the background.
 Optimized Battery Charging pauses around 80% and completes closer to when you usually unplug.
 Charge Limiting features help keep the battery from sitting at 100% for hours.
 Adaptive Power adjusts performance and background activity to stretch battery life.
 Leave these features on unless you have a specific need to disable them. They're designed to manage everyday charging without you having to think about it.
 Try not to run the battery to 0%
 Lithium-ion batteries don't need full drain cycles, and hitting 0% too often can add stress. Plug in when you drop into low percentages instead of waiting until the phone shuts off. It's fine if it reaches 0% once in a while; just avoid making it a habit.
 Use safe, high-quality chargers and cables
 Poor-quality accessories can cause unstable power, slower charging, or overheating. Use chargers and cables from trusted brands and look for USB-C Power Delivery (PD) support. For wireless charging, choose MagSafe or Qi2-certified products that list iPhone compatibility. Replace any damaged cables as soon as you spot fraying or bent connectors.
 Overnight charging is okay with protections on
 It's safe to charge overnight as long as the phone can stay cool. With features like Optimized Battery Charging, the phone slows down near the top of the charge and finishes closer to your usual wake-up time.
 Conclusion
 Knowing how to charge iPhone 17 gives you more control over speed, convenience, and long-term battery health. Whether you prefer fast USB-C, MagSafe/Qi2 magnetic wireless charging, or a power bank on busy days, the iPhone 17 handles each method well as long as you use quality accessories and keep heat in check. And if you want reliable chargers that match the phone's full charging potential, Anker offers several options that pair perfectly with Apple's latest lineup.
 FAQs
 Does iPhone 17 come with a charger?
 No, it doesn't. Like recent iPhone models, the iPhone 17 doesn't include a power adapter in the box. You'll find a USB-C to USB-C cable, but you'll need to use your own charger or buy one separately. Any quality USB-C charger that supports USB Power Delivery (PD) will work safely with the phone, though you'll get the fastest speeds with a 40W or higher adapter.
 Can I charge my new iPhone 17 with an old charger?
 Yes, in most cases, you can. If your old charger has a USB-C port and supports USB Power Delivery (PD), it will charge the iPhone 17 without issue. Older 20W-35W chargers still work well, though a 40W or higher adapter will deliver the fastest speeds (about 50% in roughly 20 minutes).
 If your charger uses USB-A, you'll need a USB-A to USB-C cable, but charging will be slower. Lightning cables from older iPhones won't fit the new port.
 Can I use an old USB cable on the new iPhone?
 It depends on the type. The iPhone 17 uses USB-C, so Lightning cables from older iPhones no longer fit. If you already own USB-C to USB-C cables, for example, from a recent iPad or MacBook, you can reuse them. Just make sure they're in good condition and support USB-PD to ensure safe, efficient charging.
 What is the best way to charge the iPhone 17?
 To charge your iPhone 17 series, the best way is to use a 40W or higher USB-C Power Delivery charger with a high-quality USB-C cable for the fastest and safest charging. Choose Apple or certified Anker USB-C PD chargers for iPhone 17 to prolong lifespan, while MagSafe or Qi2 wireless chargers at 25W (also known as Qi2.2) are also ideal for convenient daily top-ups.

 iPhone 17 Models Likely to Support 25W Wireless Third-Party Chargers
 Tuesday July 15, 2025 8:31 am PDT by Tim Hardwick 
 Apple's forthcoming iPhone 17 models are likely to support up to 25W wireless charging using a variety of third-party MagSafe charging accessories, thanks to compatibility with the next-generation Qi 2.2 wireless charging standard.
Currently, iPhones featuring MagSafe use Qi 2, the Wireless Power Consortium's (WPC) widely supported second-generation charging standard. With third-party chargers, Qi 2 maxes out at 15W – although iPhone 16 models do support upgraded 25W MagSafe charging using an official 30W Apple charger .
 That limitation is likely to change with the iPhone 17 models, which are expected to support Qi 2.2, based on regulatory filings for updated MagSafe Chargers on Taiwan's NCC certification website. It was originally believed – and widely reported – that the WPC's Qi 2.2 standard would support up to 50W output. However, this turned out to be based on incorrect information. Qi 2.2 officially supports up to 25W . 
Expect iPhone-compatible third-party Qi 2.2 chargers to become increasingly prevalent as we edge closer to the launch of the iPhone 17 lineup in September. For example, Ugreen has already announced its MagFlow Magnetic Power Bank, which it says is the first in the world to receive official Qi 2.2 certification from the WPC. The power bank is set to launch across the US, Europe, and Southeast Asian markets in the third quarter of this year.
 In addition to faster charging, Qi 2.2 offers improved magnetic alignment and charging efficiency compared to its predecessor. The standard also features backward compatibility with older Qi chargers.

 Wireless charging can definitely have an impact on battery life, though many factors must be considered. 
 By Calvin Wankhede 
 •
 Jun 8, 2025 — 9:59 PM ET 
 •
 •
 Ryan Haines / Android Authority
 Add Android Authority on Google: 
 Preferred Source Google Discover 
 Most premium and upper mid-range smartphones ship with the ability to wirelessly charge these days. The feature allows you to keep your battery topped up throughout the day without the hassle of constantly plugging in every time you set down your phone. As convenient as this feature might be, however, should you worry about wireless charging affecting your smartphone’s battery’s health? Let’s break it down.
 QUICK ANSWER 
 All things being equal, wireless charging isn’t significantly more harmful to your device or its battery than wired charging. That said, charging your device wirelessly generates more heat, which reduces battery health in the long term. Samsung, Google, and other manufacturers sell wireless chargers with a built-in cooling fan to alleviate heating issues. 
 Is wireless charging good or bad for battery health?
 Rita El Khoury / Android Authority
 Charging a battery in any way does wear it out to some extent. External factors like heat can accelerate this wear, reducing the battery’s capacity in the long term. And that’s exactly where wireless charging performs worse than conventional wired charging.
 While charging, not all the power pulled from a wall outlet ends up reaching your device’s battery. It’s widely understood that the efficiency of wireless charging is around 80%. That figure could drop as low as 50% in the real world, depending on how well you align the coils in the charger and smartphone. Needless to say, wired charging is far more efficient since a copper wire conducts electricity extremely well and there’s no physical gap. We’ve compared 100W wired and wireless charging to confirm this hypothesis in the real world.
 Coming back to wireless charging, the energy that doesn’t make it to your device gets converted into heat. And as we highlighted already, continued exposure to heat will degrade your device’s battery. Moreover, if you use a thick case with your smartphone, it could prevent it from cooling down quickly enough.
 Wireless charging has the potential to generate excess heat, which can negatively impact battery health. 
 You’ll find that some of the best wireless chargers include a cooling fan to keep temperatures under control. The vast majority of public and in-car wireless chargers don’t include one, but these are typically restricted to lower power outputs like 5W. At such low wattages, there’s little heat generated so your device won’t overheat either. The downside is that it will take several hours to fully recharge your phone.
 We expect wireless charging efficiency to improve in the coming years with the release of the updated Qi2 standard in 2024 flagship smartphones. It adds magnets around the wireless charging coil, which helps minimize losses due to improper placement.
 All things considered, you don’t have to worry much about wireless charging causing smartphone battery degradation . Even if your phone does somehow get dangerously hot, modern battery management systems can communicate with the charger to either reduce power output or stop charging altogether. After all, the same protections exist for wired charging too.
 Tips for long smartphone battery life
 Robert Triggs / Android Authority
 All smartphones have built-in measures to prevent damage from wireless charging, but here are a few steps you can take to lower the risk of damage even further.
 1. Top up your battery frequently
 Studies have proven that smartphone batteries last the longest when they’re kept between 20 and 80% of their maximum capacity. In other words, if you want to conserve battery health for as many years as possible, don’t charge to 100% regularly.
 Instead of charging your phone overnight, you could top up the battery in short bursts throughout the day. Samsung and a handful of other manufacturers even offer the ability to limit charging to 85% for this very reason. Finally, if you won’t be using a battery-powered electronic device for a few weeks, don’t leave it fully charged for the same reason.
 2. Keep your device cool
 While ambient temperature isn’t always in your control, exposing your smartphone to extreme heat (or even cold) can lead to rapid battery degradation. Some scenarios that put undue stress on the battery include leaving your phone exposed to the sun or placing it under a pillow while fast charging.
 Apple recommends avoiding temperatures higher than 95° F or 35° C and states that the ideal range is much lower than that at 62° to 72° F or 16° to 22° C.
 3. Use super fast charging sparingly
 While the impact of fast charging on battery health is not as well known, our own testing has shown that pushing more power increases heat output. The amount of heat generated varies depending on the smartphone in question, though, as no two technologies work the same. Some Android skins, like Samsung’s One UI, allow you to disable fast wireless charging within the battery settings menu.
 If you’re using wireless charging over several hours, it’s worth turning off fast wireless charging so that the heat output remains low.
 4. Don’t use wireless charging overnight
 If you have plenty of time to spare, like when you charge overnight, consider plugging your phone into the wall rather than relying on wireless tech. Moreover, try using a 10W or 18W fast charging brick as these don’t generate nearly as much heat. You don’t always need 65W or 150W charging, after all. You can also step all the way down to 5W if you don’t care about charging time at all. The same applies to fast wireless charging, as discussed above.
 If all else fails, don’t forget that it’s possible to replace your smartphone battery . It can be a hassle if you don’t live near a repair center but it’s a lot cheaper than a brand new smartphone. Most brands charge less than $100 including taxes and labor. If you plan on using your device for five years or longer, it’s probably worth replacing the battery around the three-year mark.
 FAQs
 Is it OK to leave phone on wireless charger overnight? Yes, you can leave your phone on a wireless charger overnight but it’s recommended to turn off fast charging to prolong battery health.
 What are the disadvantages of wireless charging? Wireless charging has a few disadvantages compared to wired, namely increased heat production which can lower battery health in the long term.

charging. This is part of Apple’s system strategy to protect the battery and extend its lifespan. Real-time 
power output is not always shown, but charging remains safe, stable, and effective, with no negative 
impact on your device.

The wireless charger distributes optimal power to Apple Watch and TWS earbuds. These devices are 
designed with internal limits, typically capping input at 5W or less. Even when using a higher-wattage

automatically synchronize with standard time without needing manual input.

Use the included anti-slip sticker to keep your watch steady while charging. It will not interfere with

Why does the product produce noise?
The internal thermoelectric cooling fan may produce some noise when it is activated to help 
dissipate heat. When the product is in Boost Mode, the noise level remains below 29 decibels, which 
is quiet enough for most everyday use. When using the charger at night, especially in a bedroom, we 
recommend switching to Sleep Mode, which turns off the fan and screen to provide a silent and dark 
charging environment.
 
Is it normal for the product to feel warm or hot?
It is normal for the charger to feel warm, especially during long charging sessions or when using your 
phone for gaming or video streaming. The metal body is designed to dissipate heat more efficiently, 
which can make it feel warm to the touch.
If the product feels too warm, try moving it to a cooler room (32 - 77°F / 0 - 25°C). Activating Ice Mode or

How to Charge Your iPhone the Right Way 
 Skip to content 
 How to Charge Your iPhone the Right Way
 How you charge your iPhone affects how long its battery lasts, but probably not in the ways you have heard. This guide covers the right charger and cable for each iPhone, how Apple’s charging limits work, when fast and wireless charging make sense, and the charging myths you can stop worrying about.
 Table of Contents
 Toggle 
 Quick Answer 
 Charge with a quality USB-C Power Delivery adapter (20W or higher for most iPhones, 40W or higher for the iPhone 17 lineup’s fastest speeds, and a 60W-capable adapter for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo), keep the phone cool, and let iOS manage the top of the charge. On the iPhone 15 and later , set a Charge Limit under Settings > Battery > Charging (80% for maximum battery longevity, higher if you need all-day runtime). On the iPhone 14 and earlier , leave Optimized Battery Charging on. Charging overnight, using your phone while it charges, and fast charging are all fine. Heat is the thing to avoid. Browse used iPhones on Swappa .
 Battery Life vs. Battery Lifespan 
 Two terms get mixed up constantly:
 Battery life is how long your iPhone runs on a single charge. See the iPhones that last longest per charge .
 Battery lifespan is how long the battery lasts before it needs replacing.
 Good charging habits mainly protect lifespan. Apple designs iPhone 15 and later batteries to keep 80% of their original capacity after 1,000 complete charge cycles, and iPhone 14 and earlier batteries after 500. How Long Do iPhone Batteries Last? Years, Cycles, and Costs explains what that means in years.
 Set Up Charge Limit or Optimized Battery Charging 
 Lithium-ion batteries age faster when they sit at 100% for long periods. Apple’s charging controls cut that time for you, so you do not have to babysit the charger. Setting one up is also on our list of new iPhone setup tips .
 iPhone 15 and Later: Charge Limit
 Open Settings > Battery > Charging .
 Choose a Charge Limit from 80% to 100%, in 5% steps.
 Your iPhone charges to within a few percent of the limit, then stops. If the battery drops more than 5% while it is still plugged in, charging resumes. It will occasionally charge to 100% anyway to keep its battery estimates accurate. That is normal.
 Which limit should you pick? Choose 80% if you usually end the day with charge to spare and want the battery to last as many years as possible. Choose 90%, 95%, or 100% if you need every bit of runtime. At 100%, the iPhone uses Optimized Battery Charging, which learns your routine and finishes charging shortly before you usually unplug. iOS may also suggest a limit based on your habits, such as 95%, if it thinks one will help.
 iPhone 14 and Earlier: Optimized Battery Charging
 Go to Settings > Battery > Battery Health & Charging and make sure Optimized Battery Charging is on. Your iPhone learns your daily routine, holds at 80% overnight, and finishes charging before you normally unplug it. It needs about two weeks of regular charging to learn your routine, so do not expect it to kick in on day one.
 The Right Charger and Cable for Your iPhone 
 Any reputable USB-C Power Delivery (USB-PD) charger works with an iPhone; it does not have to be made by Apple. Match the wattage to your model if you want the fastest charging:
 iPhone model Port Apple’s fast charge claim Adapter you need 
 iPhone 18 Pro , 18 Pro Max USB-C Up to 50% in about 15 minutes 60W-capable adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) 
 iPhone Duo USB-C Up to 50% in about 20 minutes 60W-capable or higher 
 iPhone 17 , 17 Pro , 17 Pro Max USB-C Up to 50% in about 20 minutes 40W or higher 
 iPhone Air , iPhone 17e USB-C Up to 50% in about 30 minutes 20W or higher 
 iPhone 16 , 16 Plus , 16 Pro , 16 Pro Max , 16e USB-C Up to 50% in about 30 minutes 20W or higher 
 iPhone 15 , 15 Plus , 15 Pro , 15 Pro Max USB-C Up to 50% in about 30 minutes 20W or higher 
 iPhone 8 through iPhone 14, including the iPhone 14 , iPhone 13 , iPhone 12 , and iPhone SE (3rd gen) Lightning Up to 50% in about 30 minutes 20W or higher USB-C adapter and a USB-C to Lightning cable 
 Apple’s own option for the iPhone 18 Pro is its 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max. Third-party chargers work too if they are 60W-capable and support Adjustable Voltage Supply, which most older USB-C chargers do not.
 A few cable tips:
 Use the USB-C cable that came with your iPhone or a well-reviewed cable from a reputable brand. Cheap, uncertified cables are the most common cause of slow or flaky charging.
 For the iPhone 18 Pro’s fastest speed, the cable has to be 60W-capable too. The one in the box is.
 For Lightning iPhones, look for MFi-certified cables, which meet Apple’s standards.
 A bigger adapter is safe. Your iPhone only draws the power it can use, so a 65W laptop charger will charge any USB-C iPhone.
 Shop Used iPhones on Swappa 
 Wireless and MagSafe Charging 
 Wireless charging is convenient and safe, but it is slower than a cable and produces a bit more heat.
 iPhone model Wireless charging 
 iPhone 18 Pro , 18 Pro Max MagSafe and Qi2 up to 25W; up to 50% in about 30 minutes with a 35W or higher adapter 
 iPhone Duo MagSafe and Qi2 up to 25W; up to 50% in about 30 minutes with a 35W or higher adapter 
 iPhone 17 , 17 Pro , 17 Pro Max MagSafe and Qi2.2 up to 25W with a 30W or higher adapter 
 iPhone 16 , 16 Plus , 16 Pro , 16 Pro Max MagSafe up to 25W with a 30W or higher adapter 
 iPhone Air MagSafe and Qi2 up to 20W with a 30W or higher adapter 
 iPhone 17e MagSafe and Qi2 up to 15W with a 20W or higher adapter 
 iPhone 12 through iPhone 15 MagSafe up to 15W with a 20W or higher adapter (12W on the 12 mini and 13 mini ) 
 iPhone 16e Qi up to 7.5W, no MagSafe 
 iPhone 8 through iPhone 11 and iPhone SE Qi up to 7.5W 
 To keep wireless charging cool, use a MagSafe or Qi2-certified charger, keep the phone centered, and take off thick cases or wallets if the phone gets warm.
 Temperature: The Biggest Factor You Control 
 Heat does more damage to an iPhone battery than anything else, and the damage is permanent. Apple’s guidance:
 The ideal comfort zone is 62 to 72°F (16 to 22°C) .
 Avoid ambient temperatures above 95°F (35°C) .
 If the battery gets too warm, iOS may limit charging above 80% until it cools down.
 Some cases trap heat while charging. If your iPhone gets hot on the charger, take it out of the case.
 In practice, that means never charging in a hot car, on a sunny dashboard mount, or under a pillow. Cold is less harmful, but let a freezing phone warm up before you plug it in.
 Is It OK to Charge Your iPhone Overnight? 
 Yes. Your iPhone stops charging when it reaches its limit, so it cannot overcharge. Optimized Battery Charging and Charge Limit both reduce the time the battery spends full overnight. Just charge it somewhere that stays cool, like a nightstand rather than under a blanket.
 iPhone Charging Myths, Debunked 
 “You have to drain it to 0% before charging.” False. Deep discharges are harder on lithium-ion batteries. Charge whenever it is convenient.
 “Charging many times a day wears it out.” False. Wear is measured in total charge cycles, not how often you plug in. Four 25% top-ups equal one cycle.
 “Using your iPhone while it charges damages the battery.” False. It is fine, though heavy gaming or navigation while charging adds heat.
 “Fast charging ruins the battery.” Not in normal use. iPhones fast charge to about 50 to 80% and then slow down, and they manage heat automatically.
 “Only Apple chargers are safe.” False. Any reputable USB-C Power Delivery charger works. Avoid unbranded bargain chargers and cables instead.
 Adaptive Power and Low Power Mode 
 These settings help battery life on a single charge rather than long-term lifespan:
 Adaptive Power (iOS 26 and later on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer, including the iPhone 16e) makes small performance adjustments on days your usage runs higher than normal, and it can turn on Low Power Mode at 20%. It is on by default on the iPhone 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, and iPhone Air. On other supported models, turn it on under Settings > Battery > Power Mode . It needs about a week to learn your habits before it starts working.
 Low Power Mode cuts background activity when you need to stretch a low battery. Turn it on from Control Center or Settings > Battery.
 Storing an iPhone You Are Not Using 
 Keeping a spare iPhone in a drawer, or holding one until you sell it? Apple recommends charging it to about 50% , powering it off, and storing it somewhere cool and dry, below 90°F (32°C) . If you store it longer than six months, top it back up to 50% every six months. A phone left completely empty for months can lose capacity for good. If you plan to sell it, check the resale value of your iPhone first, then sell your iPhone on Swappa while it still holds that value.
 When Charging Habits Are Not Enough 
 Good habits slow battery aging; they do not stop it. If Battery Health shows a service recommendation or your iPhone no longer lasts a day, a battery replacement or an upgrade is the fix. To weigh the two, see the signs it’s time to upgrade . How Long Do iPhone Batteries Last? Years, Cycles, and Costs covers replacement costs, and if your iPhone will not charge at all, start with iPhone Won’t Charge? Here’s How to Fix It . For battery care across all your devices, see Battery Care: How to Extend Battery Lifespan .
 Charging Features to Look For in a Used iPhone 
 If you upgrade, used iPhones on Swappa cost far less than new, but charging features changed a lot between generations. Here is where each one starts. Prices are average Swappa sale prices for each model’s base storage tier as of October 11, 2026.
 USB-C and Charge Limit: the iPhone 15 (about $386 for 128GB) is the least expensive model with both. The iPhone 14 (about $284) still uses Lightning and Optimized Battery Charging.
 A budget model without MagSafe: the iPhone 16e (about $367 for 128GB) has USB-C and Charge Limit but only 7.5W Qi wireless charging. The iPhone 17e (about $519 for 256GB) adds MagSafe at up to 15W.
 Adaptive Power: the iPhone 15 Pro (about $487 for 128GB) is the oldest iPhone that supports it.
 25W MagSafe: every iPhone 16 model except the 16e, starting with the iPhone 16 (about $530 for 128GB).
 Fast wired charging for the money: the iPhone 17 (about $737 for 256GB) reaches 50% in about 20 minutes on a 40W adapter, the same as the iPhone 17 Pro (about $915).
 The newest models: the iPhone 18 Pro charges fastest of all, but Swappa had only a handful of listings and no sale history for it on October 11. The iPhone Duo ships October 23.
 Most iPhone listings on Swappa also show the battery health percentage, so you can compare batteries before you buy. iPhone Battery Health: What to Check on a Used iPhone explains what a good number looks like, and the Used iPhone Buyer’s Guide: Every Generation Ranked (2026) covers everything beyond charging.
 FAQ 
 Should I charge my iPhone to 80% or 100%?
 On the iPhone 15 and later, an 80% Charge Limit keeps the battery healthiest over time if you usually have charge to spare at the end of the day. If you need all-day runtime, set it higher. At 100%, Optimized Battery Charging still limits the time the battery sits full.
 Which iPhones have Charge Limit?
 The iPhone 15 and later, including the iPhone 16e, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air. The iPhone 14 and earlier use Optimized Battery Charging instead, which holds the battery at 80% overnight and finishes charging before you usually unplug.
 Is it bad to charge my iPhone overnight?
 No. iPhones stop charging when full, and Optimized Battery Charging or Charge Limit reduces time spent at 100%. Charge somewhere cool, since heat is what actually harms the battery.
 Is fast charging bad for an iPhone battery?
 Not in normal use. iPhones fast charge to around half capacity, then slow down and manage heat automatically. Fast charging in a hot environment is the combination to avoid.
 Can I use any USB-C charger with my iPhone?
 Yes, if it is a reputable USB-C Power Delivery charger. Your iPhone draws only the power it can use, so higher-wattage chargers are safe. Use 20W or higher for fast charging, 40W or higher for the iPhone 17 lineup’s fastest speeds, and a 60W-capable charger for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.
 Is wireless charging bad for an iPhone battery?
 No, but it is slower and runs a little warmer than a cable. Use a MagSafe or Qi2-certified charger, keep the phone aligned, and remove a thick case if the phone gets hot.
 What charger does the iPhone 17 need for fast charging?
 The iPhone 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max reach up to 50% in about 20 minutes with a 40W or higher USB-C adapter. For MagSafe charging at up to 25W, Apple calls for a 30W or higher adapter.
 Conclusion 
 Charging your iPhone the right way is mostly about letting it do its job: a decent USB-C charger, a Charge Limit or Optimized Battery Charging, and no heat. Do that, and the battery will last as long as it is designed to. Shopping for a used iPhone? Check the listed battery health first with iPhone Battery Health: What to Check on a Used iPhone .

 by Simon Jary 
 Contributor, Macworld 
 Updated 
 Qi2 vs. MagSafe: Which wireless charger is best for your iPhone?
 Updated 
 Oct 21, 2026 
 Summary created by Smart Answers AI 
 In summary:
 Macworld compares Qi2 and MagSafe wireless charging standards, explaining how both support up to 15W for iPhone 12 through 15, while newer iPhone 16 models can reach 25W via the latest Qi2.2 standard.
 Qi2 chargers match MagSafe speeds without expensive Apple certification fees, making them a more affordable option with broad compatibility across iPhone and Android devices.
 Matching your iPhone model to the correct charger standard appears essential for achieving maximum wireless charging efficiency.
 Not having to find the right cable or carry one around with you makes wireless charging a convenient way of charging your mobile devices—iPhone, Apple Watch, AirPods and many third-party gadgets.
 There are multiple wireless charging standards and technologies. Here we will explain the major ones— Qi , MagSafe , Qi2 and the latest Qi2 25W (aka Qi2.2 ). Knowing which is which will help you to make your charging life more efficient. Here we look at Qi2 vs MagSafe and Qi2 25W vs Qi2 and Apple’s updated 2024 version of MagSafe. Which is best for your model of iPhone?
 It’s a little more nuanced, but in general, iPhones 16, 17 and 18 (and the iPhone Duo) should now charge wirelessly at up to 25W with supporting certified Qi 2.2 chargers. Older iPhones are limited to the 15W maximum if they support certified Apple MagSafe or Qi2. Chargers that are merely “MagSafe Compatible” are usually limited to 7.5W wireless charging. Note that the iPhone Air is limited to 20W wireless, the 16e to 7.5W and 17e to 15W.
 iPhone wireless charging speeds in brief: 
 iPhone 8-11 series and 16e: Qi 7.5W . 0-50% in around 90 minutes.
 iPhone 12-15 series and 17e: MagSafe 15W and Qi2 15W . 0-50% in around 45 minutes.
 iPhone Air: 20W Qi2 . 0-50% in around 40 minutes.
 iPhone 16 and 16 Pro: MagSafe 22W and Qi2.2 22W . 0-50% in around 35 minutes.
 iPhone 16 Plus, 17, 17/18 Pro, 16/17/18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo: MagSafe 25W and Qi2.2 25W . 0-50% in around 30 minutes.
 Don’t worry too much about the difference between 22W and 25W—the charging time difference will be marginal given environmental conditions such as room temperature will also make an impact.
 How does wireless charging work?
 Wireless charging uses electromagnetic induction to power your devices. The charging pad and your phone both include copper wire coils. Plug the pad into a power source and the charger’s coil generates a magnetic field. When you place your phone onto the charging pad, the phone’s coil converts that magnetic field into an electric current, thus charging the phone.
 Apple pioneered improved magnetic connection between charger and phone with MagSafe, and it’s mainly the tighter magnetic fit that drives faster and faster wireless charging.
 What is Qi2? 
 Qi2—supported by the iPhone 12 and up—speeds up wireless charging from 7.5W to 15W and makes chargers cheaper as well as more efficient. It is very like MagSafe, which is unsurprising as Apple allowed the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) to use MagSafe as the basis of Qi2.
 In short, Qi2 brings the magnetic benefits of MagSafe, but also make third-party iPhone chargers faster and potentially cheaper. Manufacturers are more likely to create new products when the market is larger (iPhone and Android) and costs should come down, too.
 Apple’s latest version of its iPhone MagSafe Charger can wirelessly charge the iPhone 16 series at 22-25W. Older iPhones can use this charger but at a 15W maximum as before. Qi2 took its time catching up, but it has now: keep reading.
 We have tested Qi2 chargers vs chargers certified as MagSafe by Apple, and can confirm that 15W Qi2 charges supporting devices at an equivalent speed to 15W MagSafe, and much faster than merely MagSafe-compatible 7.5W chargers. More details of our wireless charging speed tests below.
 Belkin first announced two Qi2 magnetic wireless charging devices in September 2023. Belkin
 What is Qi2.2 25W?
 The latest Qi2 25W standard (officially Qi 2.2) matches Apple’s 25W wireless charging speed. We have tested many 25W chargers, including the Belkin 25W UltraCharge Pro 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Dock , Ugreen MagFlow Power Bank , 25W Baseus PicoGo AM52 Power Bank and ESR’s 25W CryoBoost 3-in-1 Charging Station among others.
 Samsung waited until its Galaxy S26 Ultra to jump on the fast magnetic wireless charging bandwagon with Qi2 25W, and Google was first out of the Android blocks with Qi2 25W compatibility with its Pixel 10 Pro XL . The lesser Google Pixel 10 Pro is pegged back at 15W Qi2. Google calls its version of Qi2 “PixelSnap”.
 Wireless charging from Qi to Qi2.2
 First, let’s look at the original Qi, which all iPhones post iPhone 8 support.
 Foundry
 What is Qi wireless charging?
 Qi is a Chinese word that means “energy flow”. Pronounced “chee”, Qi is the basic and most popular wireless charging standard, launched in 2008 but not seen on an iPhone until 2017’s iPhone 8.
 Note that plain Qi2 has little magnetic connection between phone and charger so is less efficient at transferring power as more is wasted depending on the placement of the phone on the charger. Better magnetic attachment and therefore faster charging arrived with MagSafe and Qi2.
 Apple continues to support the Qi wireless charging standard with its most recent iPhones—and the iPhone 12 and later models are compatible with Qi2, more on which later. This means that iPhones from the iPhone 8 onwards can be placed on a Qi-compatible charger to start charging without a cable. (Of course, the Qi charging pad or stand itself has to be connected via a cable to a power charger.)
 While wireless charging means less wear and tear to your devices, it is not as efficient as charging via a cable (wired charging) as some of the energy is lost between the charging pad and the device placed on it.
 Qi users will know that you have to ensure your device is placed in exactly the right alignment for fast wireless charging to take place. Place the iPhone on the pad incorrectly and you end up either charging much more slowly or not at all. Many of us have dropped a phone on a Qi charger only to find out later that it wasn’t in the right place and so annoyingly never started charging—a problem largely solved by Apple’s MagSafe.
 While Qi’s maximum wireless charge is 15W, Apple’s iPhone supports only 7.5W via Qi.
 Which iPhones use Qi? 
 Qi charging is built into the iPhone 8, X, XR, XS, SE, 11, 12, 13, and 14 families. The iPhone 15/16/17/18 and Air/Duo work with Qi but are rated as Qi2; see later. The outlier is the curious iPhone 16e that goes all the way back to plain old Qi; the 17e is fine.
 Foundry
 What is MagSafe wireless charging?
 Apple’s magnetic MagSafe iPhones contain a ring of magnets built around its Qi charging coil. As a result, you can magnetically clamp charging accessories onto the iPhone. In fact, you can magnetically attach non-charging accessories, such as wallets and mounts, too.
 MagSafe—from 2020’s iPhone 12 on—makes missing the charging pad’s coils much less likely with its ring of magnets quickly finding the charging alignment sweet spot—on a compatible charger—so you will always connect and less energy is wasted.
 Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) technology uses magnets to perfectly align the coils of the wireless charging transmitter and receiver before transferring power.
 iPhones can work with wireless chargers that are either MagSafe certified by Apple (“made for MagSafe”) or are compatible with MagSafe—plus less sophisticated Qi chargers.
 Certified MagSafe chargers can supply up to 25W to the iPhone, while merely MagSafe compatible chargers are limited to 7.5W , but compatible chargers are usually cheaper. That 25W charging speed is currently limited to the iPhone 16 and 17 ranges and Apple’s own MagSafe Charger . iPhones 12/13/14/15 max out at 15W using MagSafe. The iPhone Air won’t charge faster than 20W wirelessly. In fact, the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro are pegged back at 22W, while the larger 16 Plus and 16 Pro Max support the while 25W. The 16e is out of the picture at just 7.5W and the 17e makes it to 15W. 
 (Note that the iPhone 12 mini only charges at 12W with MagSafe.)
 We have tested the best MagSafe chargers for iPhones and the best MagSafe power banks for iPhones. This reviews roundup now also includes 15W Qi2 and 25W Qi2.2 chargers as they arrive to market.
 Some thicker cases get in the way of MagSafe wireless charging so make sure your iPhone’s case is MagSafe compatible—see our roundup of the best iPhone 15 Cases , best iPhone 16 cases , best iPhone 17 cases and best iPhone 18 cases .
 Wireless charging is great, but it’s not as fast as wired charging. For truly fast iPhone charging, use a cable connected to at least a 20W USB-C charger. For the iPhone 15 and later that means a USB-C to USB-C cable ; for older iPhones you’ll need a USB-C to Lightning cable . A USB-A to Lightning cable won’t offer iPhone fast charging. Click here for more iPhone fast-charging tips .
 Somewhat confusingly, MagSafe is also the name for Apple’s wired-charging standard for its MacBooks—connecting the charging cable to the MacBook’s MagSafe port via magnets, meaning it is not only easy to connect but, if accidentally disconnected, it pops out rather than dragging your laptop to the floor. This version of MagSafe is magnetic and safe and has a charging connection for MacBooks but is not wireless. We explain the difference between MagSafe on Mac and MagSafe on iPhones in our Complete guide to Apple MagSafe: What is MagSafe? 
 Which iPhones use MagSafe? 
 MagSafe wireless charging is built into the iPhone 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18 families, with the exception of the 16e. It’s also supported by the iPhone Air and iPhone Duo.
 Foundry
 What is Qi2 wireless charging?
 Qi2 (“chee too”) is the latest version of the Qi “energy flow” wireless charging standard, and it’s supported by all iPhones from the iPhone 12.
 Famed for its “Not Invented Here” strategy, Apple can be quite precious about adopting other technical standards. It has a long history of rejecting any idea that didn’t originate within Apple itself. However, thankfully Apple has cooperated with the creation of Qi2 to the extent that in effect it gave the Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) MagSafe to use as the basis for Qi2’s Magnetic Power Profile that defines how the new generation Qi works. Apple is a WPC “steering member” and chair of the board of directors.
 So what is Qi2 and why is it so great?
 Think of Qi2 as not just MagSafe for Android, but MagSafe benefits for all compatible wireless charging products.
 Qi2 means chargers won’t have to be certified by Apple to support 15W charging. They should, however, meet the technical demands of the WPC. In short, a Qi2 charger will deliver twice as fast charging as “MagSafe-compatible” chargers.
 As MagSafe certification costs manufacturers a fee to Apple, removing this should result in cheaper chargers that match Apple-certified chargers in terms of speed. 
 Which iPhones use Qi2? 
 Qi2 wireless charging works with all iPhones 12. and onwards, except the 16e.
 Simon Jary / Foundry
 What is Qi2 25W wireless charging?
 Qi2 25W is the latest version of the Qi “energy flow” wireless charging standard. Its technical name is Qi2.2.
 It started rolling out in wireless charging products from the mid-2025 and is now seen in many new wireless charging products.
 So what is Qi2 25W and why is it so great?
 Qi2 25W means chargers can support up to 25W wireless charging. They have to meet the technical demands of the WPC. In short, a Qi2 25W charger will deliver 10W more power than Qi2 and 3.3 times as fast charging as MagSafe-compatible chargers.
 The use of a Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) provides better alignment but also reduces magnetic field leakage caused by misalignment. This minimizes the build-up of heat and ensures optimal charging efficiency. A ±0.5mm magnetic alignment precision improves charging efficiency by “up to 40%”, according to manufacturer Baseus.
 Qi2 25W products also feature next-generation thermal regulation with stricter 40°C surface limits and enhanced coil layouts. This ensures that less energy is wasted and provides 15% better charging efficiency—even in motion or with slight misalignment.
 Which iPhones use Qi2 25W?
 Qi2 25W wireless charging will work with the iPhone 16 family and later (except the 16e and 17e). The iPhone Air supports Qi2 25W but only up to 20W, which is likely caused by the super-thin phone’s thermal management. The iPhone 16 and 16 Pro can make it to only 22W according to Apple. The iPhone Duo does support 25W Qi2.2.
 For Qi2 25W to work at full 25W supporting iPhones must have installed at least iOS 26 or later.
 Which is best MagSafe, Qi2 or Qi2 25W?
 First, MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2 25W are all better than plain Qi. Owing in large part to their magnetic connection, they are more efficient and definitely offer faster wireless charging than Qi.
 For all extents and purposes, Qi2 looks pretty identical to MagSafe so iPhone 12/13/14/15 users can choose between MagSafe or Qi2 without fear. iPhone 16/17/18/Air/Duo owners, however, should look to MagSafe or Qi2 25W, as Apple’s own MagSafe Charger and soon Qi2 25W chargers can reach charging speeds of up to 25W when paired with the latest range of iPhones.
 All should clamp chargers magnetically to the iPhone in the same way and allow for between 15W and 25W wireless charging.
 Will Qi2 chargers work with MagSafe?
 Although technically very similar, Apple is likely to still require MagSafe certification for non-Qi2 products to reach 15W wireless charging. Both the charger and the device must be certified for Qi2 for it to work at 15W, in the same way as MagSafe. However, it is likely that future MagSafe-certified products will also be certified for Qi2, and post iOS 17.2 all iPhones (except 16e) will work natively with Qi2 and Qi2.2 chargers.
 For consumers it’s a win-win as Qi2 and Qi2 25W means faster wireless charging will be brought to more devices and people. For product marketers it may be a bit of a labelling nightmare until all the chargeable devices catch up with the technology: expect MagSafe Compatible (7.5W), MagSafe (15W or 25W), Qi2 15W (15W) and Qi2 25W or Qi2.2 (25W).
 Is Qi2 as fast at wireless charging as MagSafe?
 As the Wireless Power Consortium used Apple technology to build the Qi2 specification, it is true that Qi2 matches MagSafe for speed. Both can charge at up to 15W and use the largely same magnetic attachment tech. Note the 25W charging potential of the Apple MagSafe Charger and iPhone 16/17, plus the same charging speed from Qi2 25W.
 The first Qi2 charger we tested and reviewed at Macworld was the Anker MagGo 3-in-1 Wireless Charging Station . We tested its Qi2 wireless charging speed by charging an iPhone 15 Pro all the way to a 100% full charge, and taking timings at 30%, 50% and 80%. We did the same using a Apple’s own MagSafe Charger and also via a straight wired USB-C connection.
 The fastest way to charge an iPhone is via a wired connection: USB-C to Lightning for iPhones older than the iPhone 15, and USB-C to USB-C for the iPhone 15 and later. The average wired-charging time in our tests was 25 minutes to 50%, 55 minutes to 80% and 70 minutes to 100%.
 Our wireless charging tests for officially Apple-certified MagSafe chargers (using Apple’s own Wireless Charger) and for Qi2 magnetic wireless charging (using the Anker MagGo) had remarkably similar timings. There was some variance either way but also small differences using the same charger so we are confident that using these two magentic wireless charging technologies came up with the same basic results on average: 45 minutes to 50%, 90 minutes to 80% and 115 minutes to 100%. 
 In summary, then, MagSafe and Qi2 charging at 15W results in the same times and so can be considered equal—except for the 25W MagSafe potential of the iPhone 16/17–and the same from Qi2 25W now it is released. And, again as expected, merely MagSafe-compatible chargers took twice as long as the 15W chargers: 45 minutes to 30%, and 90 minutes to 50%.
 Our tests demonstate that Qi2 25W will charges an iPhone 16 Pro from 0–50% in just over 30 minutes—manufacturers often claim 25 minutes but that is under clinical conditions. In Macworld’s real-world tests 32-34 minutes is the average. In comparison, a Qi2 15W charger generally takes about 45 minutes to reach the same level—this would work out as the 25W option being around 45% faster than the 15W chargers. Wireless charging depends on many factors, such as device settings, usage during charging, and ambient temperature.
 Don’t concern yourself greatly about the 22W limit of the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro. The 3% difference between that and 25W is marginal.
 Why does phone charging speed slow down as the battery gets fuller?
 Batteries charge slower the fuller they get, especially in the last 10–20% of charging. The fuller the battery is, the slower it absorbs energy.
 To start with, a Lithium-Ion battery accepts whatever current it can, but as the battery gets closer to being full it accepts less current, and so the power being transferred tapers off.
 Imagine you were filling up a glass with water. You can start with the faucet or tap at full blast, but as the glass gets fuller, you have to slow the flow down to avoid the water spilling over, until eventually just a trickle of water goes in as you try to get it right up to the brim.
 If the battery didn’t charge this way and instead filled up at full blast till reaching 100%, it would get very hot and you’d risk damaging it to the point it might explode!
 Slowing down the charge when the battery is getting closer to full also increases the number of charge cycles a battery can go through before it permanently loses capacity.
 Taking advantage of this, if you need to charge quickly, stop at 80%, use the device for a while and then top back up to 80% before the charging speed starts to slow.

 iPhone 17 40W Charging Upgrade
 If you have been using the same 20W chargers that became standard with the iPhone 12, the iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, and iPhone 17 Pro Max now support up to 40W wired charging over USB-C. With the right charger and cable, these models can reach a 50% charge in about 20 minutes, a meaningful jump over previous generations.
 Important : iPhone Air continues to support up to 20W wired charging. 
 How iPhone 17 Reaches 40W Speeds
 The iPhone 17 family uses USB-C Power Delivery (PD) to negotiate charging speeds. When you plug in, the charger lists what it can supply and the iPhone selects the highest safe level.
 iPhone 17, 17 Pro, Pro Max : up to 40W
 iPhone Air : capped at 20W, even with a higher-wattage charger
 Faster charging is reserved for the iPhone 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max; iPhone Air continues with the familiar 20W speeds.. 
 Cable Compatibility
 Any USB-C to USB-C cable rated for 60W (3A) is enough for every iPhone 17 model.
 100W+ (5A) e-marked cables are not required for charging the phone, though they are useful if you also charge a laptop with the same cable.
 Look for USB-IF certified cables; they are tested for safety and performance.
 For a deeper dive, see our USB cables ultimate guide .
 Charging Speeds in Real Use
 Apple's charging curve delivers higher speeds in the 1-50% range, then tapers off to protect the battery.
 iPhone 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max: stable charging close to 40W sustained, making short top-ups significantly faster.
 iPhone Air: up to 20W wired, consistent with previous generations.
 iPhone 17 Wireless Charging
 The iPhone 17 family also gets a wireless charging upgrade. Here is what each model supports:
 iPhone 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max: up to 25W wireless on a Qi2.2 (also called Qi2 25W) charger or magnetic power bank. This is the biggest wireless jump since MagSafe launched.
 iPhone Air: up to 20W on MagSafe and up to 20W on Qi2 wireless chargers. (Verified 2026-05-05 against apple.com/iphone-air/specs/. The "15-20W" range used in the original blog post was imprecise; both MagSafe and Qi2 cap at 20W flat on iPhone Air.)
 To take advantage of 25W wireless on the iPhone 17 Pro models, you need a Qi2.2-certified charger or magnetic power bank. Standard MagSafe chargers will still work, but they cap at 15W. See our wireless power banks for Qi2 and MagSafe-compatible options.
 Requirements for iPhone 17 Fast Charging
 A USB-C PD 3.1 (or newer) charger rated 40W or higher 
 For iPhone 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max: a 40W to 65W charger gives the phone room to negotiate its ideal profile.
 For iPhone Air: anything above 20W will not increase speed.
 A USB-C to USB-C cable rated for 60W (3A) or higher> 
 100W (5A) e-marked cables are optional.
 USB-IF certified is preferred.
 Smart charging habits 
 Plug directly into the wall.
 Remove thick cases during fast charging.
 Start your charge between 1% and 50% for the fastest boost.
 Belkin's BoostCharge Pro USB-C wall chargers and 100W USB-C cables meet all of the above.
 Benefits in Daily Use
 iPhone 17 family : a 10-15 minute top-up gives a much bigger battery boost than older models.
 iPhone Air : still benefits from quick charging, capped at 20W.
 One-charger travel kit : a compact PD charger can fast-charge your iPhone 17 Pro and still power a laptop.
 Battery health : Apple's charging curve avoids the stress of extreme wattages while still being faster than older models.
 Compatibility with Existing Chargers
 20W chargers : work with every model. iPhone Air gets its full speed; iPhone 17 family will charge slower than 40W.
 30W chargers : work for iPhone 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max but will not enable the full 40W ceiling.
 65W and higher chargers: fully supported and safe. PD ensures the iPhone only draws what it needs.

 FAQs
 Does iPhone 17 include a charger?
 No. The box includes the phone and a USB-C to USB-C cable. You will need a separate USB-C PD charger.
 Do I need a special 40W cable? 
 No, any 3A/60W USB-C to USB-C cable works for fast charging. 5A e-marked cables are optional and only needed if you also charge a laptop with the same cable.
 Can I use my MacBook charger?
 Yes. USB Power Delivery ensures the iPhone only draws what it needs, even from a 100W charger.
 Is wireless charging catching up?
 On the iPhone 17, 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max, yes. Qi2.2 at 25W is much closer to wired speeds. On iPhone Air, wireless tops out at 20W.

Apple iPhone 17 smartphone review - The best iPhone of the year is unbelievably close to an iPhone Pro - Notebookcheck Review 
 Verdict on the Apple iPhone 17
 The Apple iPhone 17 comes closer to the Pro models than ever before and is therefore likely to be the most interesting new iPhone for many buyers. While it is priced the same as its predecessor, it now offers twice the storage. In addition, the 6.3-inch display is not only larger and brighter, but also finally supports 120 Hz and an Always-on function. 
 The main and ultra-wide-angle cameras have also been improved, now with a resolution of 48 MP, while the resolution of the selfie camera has been increased to 18 MP. The Apple A19 gives the iPhone 17 even more power, while also improving its battery life. Charging is also faster, although at a maximum of 40 watts, it still lags far behind competitors such as the Xiaomi 15, which supports up to 90 watts.

 When it comes to USB-C speed, the iPhone 17 keeps its distance from the Pro models, as there is still only USB 2.0 instead of USB 3.0. The USB-C interface makes it possible to mirror the display content on an external monitor using an adapter.

 Software - iOS 17 and Liquid Glass
 IOS 26 officially arrives with the iPhone 17 models. In addition to its new glass look, the latest version brings a number of system improvements. For example, the photo app is now clearer, the camera app got a new user interface, while Apple Intelligence makes it possible to translate and transcribe audio in real-time. We offer a more detailed review of the latest features of iOS 26 in this article . 
 In a typical Apple manner, there is no exact information on the support period. However, users can expect at least 5 years of updates for the iPhone 17. For example, the iPhone 11 , which is already 6 years old, will still receive the update to iOS 26.
 Sustainability
 The iPhone 17 contains 30% recycled materials, including 100% recycled gold in all circuit boards developed by Apple. The battery comprises 95% recycled lithium, and the product packaging consists of 100% recycled wood fibers. All details can be found in the environmental report on the iPhone 17 . 
 For self-repair, Apple offers repair manuals and spare parts . The manufacturer accepts old devices for trade-in to help buyers save on the purchase of a new iPhone.
 Communication and GNSS - iPhone 17 with new N1 chip
 With the N1, Apple installs a radio chip from its own production in the iPhone 17. With WiFi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, NFC, and Thread, it is state-of-the-art in terms of communication technology and supports numerous mobile frequencies, including 4x4 MIMO for 5G and LTE. A second-generation UWB chip flanks the N1. 
 The WiFi 7 bandwidth of the N1 chip is limited to 160 MHz instead of the standard 320 MHz. Connected to our reference router, Asus ROG Rapture AXE11000, the iPhone 17 nevertheless achieves a very high data throughput. In the transmission test, it lags slightly behind the transfer rates of the iPhone 16 but achieves a significantly higher speed in the receiving test.

 Phone functions and voice quality - Dual eSIM possible
 A nano SIM card fits into the SIM slot of the iPhone 17, which also supports VoLTE and WiFi calling. An eSIM can also be activated, and dual eSIM operation is also possible. Additionally, the phone supports accident detection and the ability to make emergency calls via a satellite connection, features already available on the iPhone 16 . 
 The iPhone 17 scores with natural voice quality and effectively suppresses ambient noise in the test if it is not too loud. In hands-free mode, intelligibility remains high, although voices sound somewhat muffled.
 Camera - 2x 48 MP and a new center-stage selfie camera
 Photo from the selfie camera 
 The number of rear cameras remains a key distinguishing feature between the standard iPhone and the Pro models. The iPhone 17 also lacks a telephoto lens, which is why it still uses a dual setup consisting of a main and ultra-wide-angle camera. 
 However, both cameras on the iPhone 17 now have a resolution of 48 MP. This helps the ultra-wide-angle camera, in particular (12 MP on the iPhone 16), capture significantly better quality photos. It automatically switches to macro mode as soon as you get close enough to an object. 
 The main camera has not changed compared to the iPhone 16, but this is no drama, because the iPhone 17 also shoots very nice photos that are characterized by high sharpness, lots of details, realistic colors, and strong contrasts. The Apple phone records videos at up to 4K resolution and 60 frames per second, delivering image quality comparable to that of photos. The videos are also well stabilized and supported by fast autofocus. 
 The main camera, which uses a small-format equivalent focal length of 26 mm, takes 24 MP photos as standard. It can be switched to 12 MP and can also utilize the full 48 MP resolution via the resolution control, compensating for the lack of telephoto zoom by using a 2x zoom to a 52 mm focal length, which only requires the inner area of the 48 MP sensor. This works well in practice and delivers very respectable results. However, at zoom factors greater than 2x (up to 10x is possible), the image quality quickly deteriorates. 
 The revised setup also includes a new "Center Stage" selfie camera. It has a resolution of 18 MP, is used in all iPhone 17 models, delivers very good image quality, and uses a square sensor. This makes it practical to take photos and videos in landscape format even when the smartphone is held upright. 
 The selfie camera automatically adjusts the image section if there are several people in front of the lens. With the dual recording option, videos can be recorded simultaneously using both the selfie and main cameras.

 Larger, smoother, and brighter than the iPhone 16 - that's how you could summarize the new features of the display. In addition, there is no longer any class difference to the Pro models, as the iPhone 17 lineup uses the technically identical Super Retina XDR display, apart from the form factor and resolution. 
 This is perhaps the most desired improvement to the display: the iPhone 17 has a ProMotion OLED that dynamically adjusts the refresh rate to up to 120 Hz. It also offers Always-On Display functionality, which reduces the refresh rate to 1 Hz. 
 Apple has also tweaked the brightness. Instead of the previous maximum of 2000 cd/m², the display can now reach up to 3000 cd/m² for short periods outdoors. As before, Apple specifies the average brightness as 1000 cd/m² and the maximum HDR value as 1600 cd/m². With smaller, bright image sections (APL18), however, we can achieve brightness levels of up to 1587 cd/m², even with SDR content. 
 Users who react to the PWM flickering of OLED screens with headaches and other physical complaints will find the iPhone 17 accommodating with a new function. Display pulse smoothing (PWM ), which can be activated in the settings, switches the OLED panel from PWM to DC dimming. In terms of measurements, however, this makes hardly any difference, although the DC dimming signal is somewhat more even and also has a slightly smaller swing. For sensitive individuals, it is advisable to try out both dimming options before making a purchase.

 Power consumption
 In the test, the iPhone 17 charges with up to 38 watts. 
 The iPhone 17 charges via MagSafe and Qi2-compatible adapters with up to 25 watts. Wired charging is possible at a maximum of 40 watts. If you use the 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max , half of the battery capacity should be recharged within 20 minutes. 
 Small flaw: Apple does not offer this power adapter in some regions. However, this is not a bad thing, as the iPhone 17 charges just as quickly with third-party models, in our case with the Anker 317 (100 watts). The iPhone 17 is charged with up to 38 watts, and 50% of capacity was ready after 23 minutes (80% after 45 minutes). 
 To protect the battery, the charging limit can be reduced from 100 to 80 percent. Without a charging limit, the iPhone 17 is fully charged in the test in 1 hour and 24 minutes.
